items.readable_text:
Content:
The experimental probability of an event is the fraction of the time that the event occurred in an experiment.

Content:
For example, suppose we conduct an experiment in which we toss a coin [MATH: 100] times, and we find that the coin lands heads up [MATH: 44] times.

Content:
To compute the experimental probability, we need to take the number of times the coin landed heads up, and divide it by the number of times we flipped the coin:

Content:
[MATH: P(\text{head}) = \dfrac{44}{100} = 0.44.]

Content:
So, the experimental probability of getting heads is [MATH: 0.44.]

Content:
The process that we repeat (here, coin tosses) is called the trial, while the outcome that we are looking to obtain (here, a head) is an event.

Content:
In general, the formula for the experimental probability is
[MATH: \text{Experimental probability} = \dfrac{\text{number of event occurrences}}{\text{total number of trials}}.]

items.title: Calculating an Experimental Probability From Experimental Data

sections.normalized_html: Elizabeth rolled a dice [MATH: 45] times, obtaining an odd number [MATH: 36] times. Based on this data, what is the experimental probability of getting an even number?
sections.readable_text: Elizabeth rolled a dice [MATH: 45] times, obtaining an odd number [MATH: 36] times. Based on this data, what is the experimental probability of getting an even number?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Elizabeth rolled an even number a total of [MATH: 45-36 = 9 \ \text{times}.]

To compute the experimental probability, we need to take the number of times that Elizabeth rolled an even number and divide it by the number of times she rolled the die:

[MATH: P(\text{even number}) = \dfrac{9}{45} = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2]

Therefore, the experimental probability of getting an even number is [MATH: 0.2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Out of the [MATH: 200] students that Martin surveyed, [MATH: 36] of those students had blue eyes. So, the experimental probability that a student has blue eyes is [MATH: P(\text{student has blue eyes}) = \dfrac{36}{200} = 0.18.]

[MATH: n = 350\cdot P(\text{student has blue eyes}) = 350\cdot 0.18 = 63.]

Therefore, we estimate that [MATH: 63] students in Brewster Academy will have blue eyes.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The experimental probability of an event is the fraction of the time that the event occurred in an experiment.

Content:
For example, suppose we conduct an experiment in which we toss a coin [MATH: 100] times, and we find that the coin lands heads up [MATH: 44] times.

Content:
To compute the experimental probability, we need to take the number of times the coin landed heads up, and divide it by the number of times we flipped the coin:

Content:
[MATH: P(\text{head}) = \dfrac{44}{100} = 0.44.]

Content:
So, the experimental probability of getting heads is [MATH: 0.44.]

Content:
The process that we repeat (here, coin tosses) is called the trial, while the outcome that we are looking to obtain (here, a head) is an event.

Content:
In general, the formula for the experimental probability is
[MATH: \text{Experimental probability} = \dfrac{\text{number of event occurrences}}{\text{total number of trials}}.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Using Experimental Probability for Predictions

Content:
Once we've calculated the experimental probability of an event, we can use the experimental probability to predict how often the event will occur in a different experiment.

Content:
For example, suppose we flip a coin [MATH: 100] times and it lands heads up [MATH: 44] of those times. Then the experimental probability is

Content:
[MATH: P(\text{head}) = \dfrac{44}{100} = 0.44,]

Content:
and we can use this probability to predict how many times the coin will land heads up in a different experiment.

Content:
For example, suppose we are going to toss the coin [MATH: 250] times. How many times do we expect it to land heads up?

Content:
To estimate the number of occurrences of this event, we multiply the new number of tosses [MATH: (250)] by the experimental probability [MATH: (0.44)] as follows:
[MATH: n = 250\cdot P(\text{head}) = 250\cdot 0.44 \approx 110]

Content:
So, if we toss the coin [MATH: 250] times, then based on the experimental probability, we estimate that the coin will land heads up about [MATH: 110] of those times.

---

Item 3 — Example: Calculating an Experimental Probability From Experimental Data

Example Prompt:
Elizabeth rolled a dice [MATH: 45] times, obtaining an odd number [MATH: 36] times. Based on this data, what is the experimental probability of getting an even number?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Elizabeth rolled an even number a total of
[MATH: 45-36 = 9 \ \text{times}.]

To compute the experimental probability, we need to take the number of times that Elizabeth rolled an even number and divide it by the number of times she rolled the die:

[MATH: P(\text{even number}) = \dfrac{9}{45} = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2]

Therefore, the experimental probability of getting an even number is [MATH: 0.2.]

Item 7 — Example: Using Experimental Probability to Estimate the Number of Occurrences of an Event Given a Table

Example Prompt:
Martin surveyed [MATH: 200] students in New Hampton School to observe the distribution of students' eye colors. The table below shows the results of his survey.

| Eye color | Frequency |
| Brown | [MATH: 60] |
| Blue | [MATH: 36] |
| Green | [MATH: 28] |
| Gray | [MATH: 60] |
| Hazel | [MATH: 16] |

In Brewster Academy, there are [MATH: 350] students. Assuming that the eye color distribution is the same for both schools, estimate the number of students with blue eyes in Brewster Academy.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Out of the [MATH: 200] students that Martin surveyed, [MATH: 36] of those students had blue eyes. So, the experimental probability that a student has blue eyes is
[MATH: P(\text{student has blue eyes}) = \dfrac{36}{200} = 0.18.]

To find an estimate for the number of students with blue eyes in Brewster Academy, we multiply the number of students in Brewster Academy [MATH: (350)] by the experimental probability [MATH: (0.18).] When we do this, we get

[MATH: n = 350\cdot P(\text{student has blue eyes}) = 350\cdot 0.18 = 63.]

Therefore, we estimate that [MATH: 63] students in Brewster Academy will have blue eyes.
